## Causal inference and the counterfactual

**Difference-in-differences** (hereafter **DiD**) is a method of **causal inference** — it
identifies a cause-and-effect relationship. It turns on one question:
*what would have happened had the shock or policy never occurred?* From that
**counterfactual** we recover the effect of the shock or the policy.

It is the very stuff of science fiction — stories built on an alternative history or a
parallel world: *The Man in the High Castle* (P. K. Dick), *Back to the Future*,
*Doctor Strange* (Marvel), and many more.

\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{fig/sc_fi.png}
\end{center}

## What is difference-in-differences?

A policy hits **some units** at **some date**. We want its causal effect — but treated and
untreated units differ systematically, so neither a treated-vs-control comparison nor a
before-vs-after comparison is clean.

\begin{block}{The idea in one line}
Compare the \textbf{change} in the treated group to the \textbf{change} in a comparison
group. The second difference nets out fixed level differences \emph{and} common time shocks.
\end{block}

- Needs **panel** (or repeated cross-sections): the same groups, before and after.
- **Simple DiD is the TWFE model from the panel chapter** — the only new ingredient is one
  explanatory variable: a **dummy** for "treated group $\times$ after treatment". We build
  from there to the modern extensions.

## The origin: John Snow and cholera (1855)

\begin{columns}[T]
\begin{column}{0.42\textwidth}
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{fig/map_snow.png}
\end{column}
\begin{column}{0.58\textwidth}
\small
\textbf{Origin: epidemiology} --- the fight against cholera in London. Cholera was assumed
to be transmitted by \textbf{air}; John Snow (1855) argued instead that it came from
\textbf{infected water}.

\medskip
\textbf{How to prove it?} A \emph{natural experiment}. The whole city drew water from the
same point in the Thames, until a reform split the supply: some districts now received
water from \textbf{downstream} of the sewers (infected), others from \textbf{upstream}
(assumed uncontaminated).

\medskip
$\Rightarrow$ \emph{treated vs control}, \emph{before vs after} --- the first
difference-in-differences.
\end{column}
\end{columns}

## The difference-in-differences logic

The **treatment** is that some neighbourhoods now receive **uncontaminated water**. We look
at the **before vs after** for treated and untreated neighbourhoods (the **first
difference**), then take the difference **between the two groups** (the **second
difference**). Any factor that hits **both** groups at once is thereby **eliminated**.

\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.68\textwidth]{fig/did.png}
\end{center}

2. **Dynamics** — event studies and two-way fixed effects.
3. **Staggered** adoption — why naive TWFE breaks, and the modern estimators.
4. **Continuous** treatment — a "dose", and the same heterogeneity lesson.

\vfill

treatments: Cunningham, \emph{Causal Inference: The Mixtape}; Békés and Kézdi (2021).*

# The canonical $2\times2$ design

## Potential outcomes

Imagine two parallel worlds for each unit $i$:

- $Y_i(1)$ — the outcome it **would have if treated**;
- $Y_i(0)$ — the outcome it **would have if not treated**.

A **treatment indicator** $D_i\in\{0,1\}$ ($1$ = treated) selects which one we actually see:
$$ Y_i = D_i\,Y_i(1)+(1-D_i)\,Y_i(0). $$

\begin{alertblock}{The fundamental problem of causal inference}
For any unit we observe \textbf{only one} potential outcome; the other — the
\textbf{counterfactual} — is never seen.
\end{alertblock}

## The treatment effect, and the missing counterfactual

The causal effect for unit $i$ is the gap between its two worlds:
$$ \tau_i = Y_i(1)-Y_i(0). $$
A treated unit ($D_i=1$) reveals $Y_i(1)$, but its $Y_i(0)$ — what would have happened
**without** treatment — is the **missing counterfactual**.

- Individual effects are hopeless, so we target **averages over groups**.
- Notation: $\E[\,\cdot\mid D_i=1\,]$ reads "the average **among treated** units";
  $\E[\,\cdot\mid D_i=0\,]$ "the average **among untreated** units" — the bar "$\mid$" means
  "restricted to".

## Two averages: ATT and ATU

\begin{block}{Average effect on the treated (ATT) and on the untreated (ATU)}
$$ \text{ATT}=\E[\,Y_i(1)-Y_i(0)\mid D_i=1\,], \qquad
   \text{ATU}=\E[\,Y_i(1)-Y_i(0)\mid D_i=0\,]. $$
\end{block}

- **ATT** — the effect for those who **were** treated ("did the policy help its
  recipients?"). **ATU** — the effect it **would have** had on the untreated ("should we
  extend it?"). They differ when effects are heterogeneous.
- **DiD targets the ATT.** The one missing piece is the treated group's untreated
  counterfactual $\E[\,Y_i(0)\mid D_i=1\,]$ — which **parallel trends** will supply.

## The two-by-two: two differences

Two groups, two periods — we now index outcomes by time, $Y_{it}(d)$. DiD builds the
treated group's missing counterfactual by assuming it would have moved **like the
control**:

\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.6\textwidth]{fig/did_canonical.png}
\end{center}

$$ \widehat{\text{ATT}}=\underbrace{(\bar y_{T,\text{post}}-\bar y_{T,\text{pre}})}_{\text{treated change}}
   -\underbrace{(\bar y_{C,\text{post}}-\bar y_{C,\text{pre}})}_{\text{control change}} $$

## Parallel trends: the identifying assumption

\begin{columns}[T]
\begin{column}{0.64\textwidth}
\begin{alertblock}{Parallel trends}
Had the treated group \emph{not} been treated, its outcome would have changed over time by
the \textbf{same amount} as the control group. Writing $\Delta Y_i(0)$ for that change in
the \textbf{untreated} outcome:
$$ \E[\Delta Y_i(0)\mid D_i=1]=\E[\Delta Y_i(0)\mid D_i=0]. $$
\end{alertblock}
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Levels} may differ freely (fixed effects absorb them) --- only the
\textbf{trend} must match.
\item \textbf{Untestable} (it concerns an unobserved counterfactual): defend it with
pre-period evidence and economic argument --- you cannot prove it.
\end{itemize}
\end{column}
\begin{column}{0.34\textwidth}
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{fig/para.png}
\end{column}
\end{columns}

## The regression form

The $2\times2$ DiD is one OLS regression:
$$ y_{it}=\alpha+\gamma\,D_i+\lambda\,\text{Post}_t+\beta\,(D_i\times\text{Post}_t)+\varepsilon_{it}. $$

- $\gamma$ — the fixed treated-vs-control gap; $\lambda$ — the common time shock.
- **$\beta$ — the DiD coefficient $=\widehat{\text{ATT}}$** under parallel trends; the
  interaction $D_i\times\text{Post}_t$ equals $d_{it}$ (one for treated units in the post
  period, zero otherwise).
- With a panel this equals two-way fixed effects (next section).

## Example: Card and Krueger (1994)

New Jersey raised its minimum wage (1992); neighbouring Pennsylvania did not. Compare
fast-food employment across the state line.

\begin{center}
\small
\begin{tabular}{lccc}
\toprule
FTE employment & Before & After & Change\\
\midrule
New Jersey (treated) & 20.44 & 21.03 & $+0.59$\\
Pennsylvania (control) & 23.33 & 21.17 & $-2.16$\\
\midrule
\textbf{Difference-in-differences} & & & $\mathbf{+2.76}$\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

- Employment in New Jersey **rose** relative to Pennsylvania — not just "did not fall" —
  against the textbook competitive prediction.
- The cross-border design makes parallel trends plausible: similar labour markets, same
  macro shocks.

## Assumptions and threats

Beyond parallel trends, a credible DiD needs:

- **No anticipation** — units don't react before treatment, or the pre-period is
  contaminated.
- **SUTVA** (stable unit treatment value) — two parts: (i) **no interference**, one unit's
  treatment does not change another's outcome (no spillovers across the border); (ii) **one
  version** of treatment, so "treated" means the same thing for every unit.
- **Stable composition** — no differential entry/exit (attrition) changing who is in each
  group.
- **Inference** — the treatment dummy is highly **serially correlated**, so naive standard
  errors badly understate uncertainty (the Bertrand–Duflo–Mullainathan 2004 problem from
  the panel chapter) $\Rightarrow$ **cluster** by unit/group.

# Dynamics: event studies

## From the $2\times2$ to panel TWFE

With many units and periods, write the DiD as **two-way fixed effects**:
$$ y_{it}=f_i+f_t+\beta\,d_{it}+u_{it}, \qquad d_{it}=D_i\cdot\text{Post}_t. $$

- $f_i$ absorbs fixed unit differences, $f_t$ the common time shocks (recall the panel
  chapter). With **common timing** (all treated units adopt at the same date),
  $\beta=\widehat{\text{ATT}}$ — an equality that **breaks under staggered timing** (the
  staggered section).
- The static $\beta$ hides two questions: do effects **grow over time**? do **pre-trends**
  hold? $\to$ the event study.

## The event-study specification

Replace the single switch by a full set of **leads and lags** around each unit's treatment
date:
$$ y_{it}=f_i+f_t+\sum_{k\neq -1}\beta_k\,\mathbf{1}\{t-t^*_i=k\}+u_{it}. $$

- $k=t-t^*_i$ is **event time** ($t^*_i$ = unit $i$'s treatment date, called $g_i$ in the
  staggered section); $k=-1$ is the **omitted baseline**, so each $\beta_k$ is relative to
  the period just before treatment.
- $\beta_k$ for $k<0$ are **pre-trends**; for $k\ge0$ they are **dynamic treatment
  effects**. (Bin the extreme $k$ to avoid under-identified endpoints.)

## Reading the event study

\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.82\textwidth]{fig/event_study.png}
\end{center}

- **Flat, near-zero** coefficients before $0$ are consistent with parallel trends; the
  post coefficients trace the effect's **dynamics**.
- A sloping pre-period ($\beta_k\neq0$ for $k<0$) is a red flag for the design.

## A caution on pre-trends

\begin{block}{Passing a pre-trend test is reassuring, not decisive}
Tests of $\beta_k=0$ for $k<0$ often have \textbf{low power} — they miss real violations —
and conditioning on "passing" can itself distort the estimate (Roth, 2022).
\end{block}

- Treat them as **evidence**, alongside an economic case for why the trends should align.
- **Plot** the coefficients; never lean on a single $p$-value (on event-study design and
  visualization, see Freyaldenhoven et al. 2021).

# Staggered adoption

## Units adopt at different times

Most policies roll out **gradually**: unit $i$ is first treated at date $g_i$.

- Example — Emission Control Areas: Baltic (2006), North Sea (2007), North America
  (2012), Caribbean (2014).
- The natural move is the same **static** TWFE — one switch
  $d_{it}=\mathbf{1}\{t\ge g_i\}$, one coefficient:
  $$ y_{it}=f_i+f_t+\beta\,d_{it}+u_{it}. $$
- The **dynamic** form you usually see swaps the switch for leads and lags,
  $\sum_{k\neq-1}\beta_k\,\mathbf{1}\{t-g_i=k\}$ — one coefficient per event time.
- **This is where it breaks** — the static $\beta$ first (next slides), and the dynamic
  $\beta_k$ with it under staggered timing.

## The TWFE trap: forbidden comparisons

\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.72\textwidth]{fig/forbidden.png}
\end{center}

TWFE implicitly uses **already-treated** units as controls for **later-treated** ones — a
**forbidden comparison**. The already-treated "control" is still responding to its own
treatment, so its change is **not** a clean counterfactual.

## Negative weights and sign reversal

\begin{alertblock}{TWFE under heterogeneity (Goodman-Bacon 2021; de Chaisemartin \& D'Haultfœuille 2020)}
The TWFE coefficient is a weighted average of all possible $2\times2$ DiDs — and some
weights are \textbf{negative}. With heterogeneous effects, $\beta$ can even take the
\textbf{wrong sign} when every true effect is positive.
\end{alertblock}

Goodman-Bacon (2021) makes this exact:
$$ \hat\beta_{\text{TWFE}}=\sum_k w_k\,\widehat{\text{DiD}}_k,\qquad
   \textstyle\sum_k w_k=1,\ \ \text{some } w_k<0, $$
the negative $w_k$ sitting on the **forbidden** (already-treated-as-control) comparisons.

\footnotesize *A recurring theme: like the complier-weighting of \textbf{LATE} and the
\textbf{Rotemberg weights} of shift-share (IV chapter), a regression coefficient is a
weighted average of heterogeneous effects — here some weights turn negative, which is what
breaks it.*

## The building block: group-time effects

Modern estimators target the **group-time ATT** directly — the effect at time $t$ for the
cohort first treated at $g$:
$$ \text{ATT}(g,t)=\E\!\left[\,Y_{it}(1)-Y_{it}(0)\ \middle|\ g_i=g\,\right],\qquad t\ge g. $$

- The missing $Y_{it}(0)$ is estimated from **clean** controls — never- or not-yet-treated
  units (no already-treated comparisons).
- **Aggregate** to one overall number (or an event study) with transparent,
  **non-negative** weights:
  $$ \text{ATT}^{o}=\textstyle\sum_{g,t} w(g,t)\,\text{ATT}(g,t),\qquad w(g,t)\ge 0, $$
  in contrast to the TWFE decomposition above, where some weights were \emph{negative}.

## The modern estimators

\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{4.7cm} >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{5.7cm}@{}}
\toprule
Estimator & Clean comparison group\\
\midrule
Callaway \& Sant'Anna (2021) & never-treated \emph{or} not-yet-treated\\
Sun \& Abraham (2021) & interaction-weighted; never-treated (or last-treated) cohort\\
Borusyak et al. (2024) & impute $Y(0)$ from not-yet-treated (efficient)\\
de Chaisemartin \& D'Haultfœuille (2020) & consecutive periods; treatment can switch on \emph{and off}\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\normalsize

\vspace{2pt}
All replace the forbidden comparison with clean controls; they differ in the control set
and in efficiency.

## What you must compute

These estimators need the **timing** structure in the data:

- the **cohort** $g_i$ — each unit's first treatment period (treated at $t=6$ $\Rightarrow$
  $g_i=6$ on \emph{all} of its rows);
- **event time** $k=t-g_i$;
- a **never- / not-yet-treated** indicator, to define clean controls.

Software builds the comparisons for you — but you must supply $g_i$.

## Example: unilateral divorce and suicide

\begin{block}{Unilateral divorce and women's suicide (Goodman-Bacon 2021)}
US states adopted unilateral divorce at staggered dates (California 1969 \dots; a few
never). Re-analysing Stevenson \& Wolfers (2006), Goodman-Bacon shows the \textbf{TWFE}
estimate of the fall in women's suicide is \textbf{smaller} than the timing-robust one
($-3.1$ vs $-7.0$).
\end{block}

- The already-treated comparisons **attenuate** the effect toward zero — here the bias
  shrinks the estimate rather than flipping its sign (both are possible).

## Staggered event study: estimators compared

\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.54\textwidth]{fig/stag_all.png}
\end{center}

- **OLS/TWFE** (open circles) is **biased** as dynamic effects grow; the **modern
  estimators** track the truth.
- Even the **pre-period** coefficients move — each naive lead/lag is **contaminated** by
  other periods' effects (Sun \& Abraham 2021).

# Continuous treatment

## When treatment is a dose, not a switch

Often treatment has **intensity**, not just on/off:

- pollution exposure that **decays with distance** from the source;
- spending levels, tax rates, minimum-wage **levels**, regulatory **stringency**.

We then care about the effect of a **change in intensity** — not merely of treatment's
existence.

## The continuous DiD specification

With a continuous dose $D_i$ switched on after the policy:
$$ y_{it}=f_i+f_t+\beta\,(D_i\times\text{Post}_t)+u_{it}. $$

- $\beta$ is a **dose-response slope**; the target is the **dose-specific** effect
  $\text{ATT}(d\mid d)=\E[Y_{it}(d)-Y_{it}(0)\mid D_i=d]$.
- Identification needs a **stronger** parallel-trends assumption: units at \emph{every}
  dose level would have trended alike absent treatment.

\begin{block}{Callback — this \emph{is} the shift-share design (IV chapter)}
Exposure is a continuous dose; the Goldsmith-Pinkham et al. (2020) "shares view" assumption
\textbf{is} parallel trends, and the estimator pools \textbf{many DiD comparisons — one per
share}.
\end{block}

## The catch: the same heterogeneity problem

\begin{alertblock}{Continuous TWFE is fragile (Callaway, Goodman-Bacon \& Sant'Anna 2024)}
If a given dose has \textbf{different effects across units}, the TWFE slope is a
\textbf{non-convex weighted average} that mixes the dose-response with how units
\textbf{select} into doses — it need not equal any dose effect, even under parallel trends.
\end{alertblock}

- This is the **staggered problem again** — heterogeneous effects $+$ implicit comparisons
  — now across **dose levels** rather than treatment **dates** (the dose analogue of
  shift-share's **Rotemberg-weight** diagnostics).
- Fix: estimate **dose-specific** effects and aggregate transparently
  (Callaway, Goodman-Bacon \& Sant'Anna 2024; de Chaisemartin et al. 2023).

# Applied

## DiD in Python (pyfixest)

```{python}
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
import pyfixest as pf
# 1. Static TWFE (single date): beta = ATT
m = pf.feols("y ~ treatpost | id + year",
             df, vcov={"CRV1": "id"})
# 2. Event study: leads/lags, baseline k = -1
es = pf.feols("y ~ i(k, ref=-1) | id + year",
              df, vcov={"CRV1": "id"})
pf.iplot(es)             # plot beta_k with CIs
# 3. Staggered: do NOT trust plain TWFE -> use
#    pf.did2s (Gardner) or Callaway-Sant'Anna.
```

- `i(k, ref=-1)` builds the event-study leads/lags; `iplot` draws them.
- For **staggered** designs, always prefer a heterogeneity-robust estimator over raw TWFE.

## Takeaways

- DiD turns **two differences** into a causal effect; identification is **parallel
  trends** — defended, not proved.
- **Event studies** show dynamics and probe pre-trends (low power $\Rightarrow$ argue,
  don't just test).
- **Continuous** and **staggered** designs break naive TWFE under **heterogeneous
  effects**: negative weights, forbidden comparisons, possible sign reversal.
- Use **group-time** estimators with clean controls (Callaway \& Sant'Anna; Sun \&
  Abraham; Borusyak et al.; de Chaisemartin \& D'Haultfœuille).
